title: Trump Ties Saudi Nuclear Deal to Israel Normalization, Upending Agreement Signed Hours Earlier
excerpt: The president demanded Riyadh join the Abraham Accords as a condition of the civilian nuclear pact, catching his own negotiating team off guard.
body:
• President Trump conditioned a multibillion-dollar Saudi nuclear cooperation deal on Riyadh normalizing relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords — one day after it was signed.
  • The 30-year agreement, signed by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, would give U.S. companies a central role in Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear infrastructure and potentially opens the door to uranium enrichment.
  • Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has consistently refused normalization without a clear pathway to Palestinian statehood, making Trump's condition a potential dealbreaker.
  • The announcement blindsided the administration's own nuclear negotiating team, according to two sources briefed on the matter.

President Donald Trump abruptly imposed a new precondition on the United States' landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia on Thursday, declaring on Truth Social that the agreement is "totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords." The demand came less than 24 hours after the pact was formally signed.

A Deal Signed, Then Rewritten

Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the 30-year, multibillion-dollar agreement on Wednesday. Under its terms, American companies would gain a central role in developing the kingdom's civilian nuclear infrastructure, including building and operating nuclear reactors. A two-year feasibility study would assess the commercial viability of uranium enrichment on Saudi soil — a provision that had already drawn sharp criticism from members of Congress and Israeli officials.

"The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!)... will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords."

— President Donald Trump, on Truth Social

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt doubled down on the condition Thursday, stating flatly: "If they don't join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off." She added that Trump "is always the final dealmaker" and had raised the issue with Gulf allies in prior conversations, though she acknowledged the president had not spoken to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since posting the new requirement.

Why Normalization Remains a Long Shot

The Abraham Accords, brokered during Trump's first term, established formal diplomatic ties between Israel and several Arab nations, including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco. Saudi Arabia conspicuously stayed out. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has made plain — both publicly and in private diplomatic channels — that Riyadh will not normalize relations with Israel absent a concrete pathway toward Palestinian statehood and calm in Gaza.

That position has not changed. The Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment on Trump's post. For Riyadh, the calculus is straightforward: joining the accords without a Palestinian component would risk domestic backlash and undermine the kingdom's standing in the broader Islamic world.

Congressional Scrutiny Ahead

Even before Trump's Abraham Accords demand, the nuclear agreement faced a difficult path through Congress. Lawmakers have 90 session days to review the deal before it takes effect. Critics have zeroed in on the enrichment provision, arguing it undercuts Washington's leverage in nuclear negotiations with Iran and risks a proliferation cascade across the Middle East.

Israel, an undeclared nuclear power that has long opposed regional nuclear proliferation, initially viewed the deal as a setback. Two Israeli sources told CNN that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was not caught off guard by the original agreement but had intended to lobby for normalization conditions — which Trump then delivered on his own.

India's Energy Stake in the Outcome

For India, the deal's trajectory carries economic and strategic weight. Saudi Arabia is one of India's top crude oil suppliers, and any disruption to Riyadh's diplomatic positioning ripples through energy markets. A successful nuclear program could also reshape Saudi Arabia's long-term energy mix, potentially affecting global oil supply dynamics. New Delhi maintains strong ties with both Riyadh and Tel Aviv, making the normalization question a delicate diplomatic puzzle for Indian policymakers as well.

What Comes Next

The deal now exists in a kind of diplomatic limbo: signed but conditional, celebrated but contested. Congressional review will proceed regardless of the Abraham Accords question, but Trump's intervention has introduced a variable that neither the negotiating teams nor Saudi officials appear to have anticipated. Whether Riyadh moves toward normalization — or walks away — will determine whether the agreement survives its first week.
